title: Counter-Model
body:
A **counter-model** proves an argument invalid by exhibiting an interpretation that makes every
premise true and the conclusion false. An interpretation is a domain of objects plus an
assignment of meanings to each predicate and constant.

```
Claim:  ∀x (Cx → Mx),  ∃x Mx   ⊨   ∃x Cx        (that anything is a cat)

Counter-model:
    domain = {1}
    C: nothing in the domain is C
    M: 1 is M

    premise 1:  ∀x (Cx → Mx)   true, since nothing is C, every conditional is vacuous
    premise 2:  ∃x Mx          true, since 1 is M
    conclusion: ∃x Cx          false, since nothing is C
```

The argument is therefore invalid, and one model settles it permanently.

This exists because a failed derivation proves nothing: no proof found could mean no proof
exists, or could mean the prover missed it. A counter-model is positive evidence in the other
direction, and it is the same technique as the single counterexample that disproves a universal
claim in [[DISCRETE MATH]], with the counterexample being an entire small world.

Small domains do most of the work. A one-element or two-element domain refutes the majority of
invalid arguments in the course, so start there.
